strengths: Clear and well-motivated central insight: fixed token order imposes a restrictive inductive bias for AR-based generative classification, illustrated convincingly via Figure 1 and the per-token discriminative likelihood/accuracy analyses in Section 5 (Figs. 3-5).
The proposed order-marginalization scheme (Jensen lower bound over K sampled orders) is simple, well justified empirically, and clearly derived from the any-order RandAR formulation.

Extensive and fair experimental protocol: models are matched in architecture, size, resolution and token count across AR, diffusion, joint-EBM and discriminative baselines; missing checkpoints are reproduced following official implementations, and the authors specifically tune diffusion baselines (loss weighting, noise-sample averaging) to ensure they are not under-optimized (Appendix C, D).

Strong and broad empirical evidence: consistent gains over diffusion classifiers and other AR classifiers (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC) across ImageNet-Val and multiple OOD/corruption benchmarks (IN-R/S/A/C), plus real-world distribution-shift evaluation on WILDS (Camelyon17, CelebA, FMoW), and efficiency-accuracy curves showing up to 25x speed-up versus DiT.

First comparison of generative classifiers against strong SSL discriminative baselines (DINOv2), showing competitive rather than merely academic performance, which is a meaningful contribution to the ongoing debate on GC viability.
Thorough ablations on tokenizer choice, noise augmentation, likelihood estimation strategy, and per-token contribution analysis (Appendix B), improving reproducibility and interpretability.
Honest error analysis comparing failure modes of RandAR vs. DINOv2, adding useful qualitative insight beyond aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is primarily an application/analysis of an existing any-order AR model (RandAR) rather than a new architecture or training method; the order-marginalization idea, while effective, is a relatively straightforward Monte Carlo/Jensen bound over an already-trained capability.

The justification for why the Jensen lower bound outperforms the direct order-marginal likelihood is largely hypothesized rather than rigorously analyzed ("we hypothesize that the lower bound largely outperforms... because RandAR was trained directly on Equation 5"), leaving the theoretical grounding somewhat underdeveloped.

A key practical limitation acknowledged only in the conclusion (compute scaling with number of classes, since separate forward passes are needed per class and per sampled order) is not empirically analyzed for classification tasks with very large label spaces, limiting insight into practical scalability beyond ImageNet's 1000 classes.

In-domain accuracy still trails DINOv2 (particularly on IN-A), and the paper's framing of "competitive" performance, while defensible, could benefit from more discussion of when generative classifiers would be preferred in practice given their added inference cost even after the reported efficiency gains relative to diffusion.

Evaluation on 2K subsets of some validation/OOD sets (necessitated by compute cost) could raise minor concerns about statistical robustness of fine-grained comparisons, despite the authors' claim that larger subsets yield similar results.

Model scale is limited to L/XL variants; it remains unclear whether the reported trends (order-marginalization benefits, relative gains over diffusion) persist at larger scales or with more modern tokenizers/architectures.

strengths: Identifies and clearly demonstrates an underexplored issue in AR-based generative classification: fixed token order imposes a restrictive inductive bias, illustrated convincingly in Fig. 1 and analyzed further via per-token accuracy/likelihood studies (Figs. 3-5).

Extensive and fairly controlled experimental comparison across multiple paradigms (discriminative, diffusion, joint energy-based, fixed-order AR) at matched architecture/resolution/token-count, spanning ID and multiple OOD benchmarks (IN-R/S/A/C), plus WILDS distribution-shift datasets.

Strong efficiency results: the proposed order-marginalized AR classifier achieves better accuracy than diffusion classifiers while requiring up to 25x fewer forward passes, and the accuracy-vs-runtime Pareto plot (Fig. 6) is a useful, direct comparison.

Good ablations supporting design choices: lower bound vs. direct order-marginal likelihood (Table 5), tokenizer robustness/noise augmentation (Tables 3-4), and diffusion classifier weighting/noise-averaging ablations (Appendix C-D) that strengthen the fairness of baselines.

First systematic comparison of generative classifiers against strong SSL discriminative baselines (DINOv2), providing a more meaningful benchmark than prior comparisons to plain supervised classifiers.
Reasonable transparency about implementation details, hyperparameters, and reproduced baselines in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is fairly incremental: it largely amounts to applying an existing any-order AR model (RandAR) with Monte Carlo averaging of log-likelihoods over K sampled orders; no new architecture, training objective, or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

The key empirical choice of using the Jensen's-inequality lower bound instead of the true order-marginal likelihood is justified only post-hoc/heuristically ("RandAR was trained on this objective"), without deeper theoretical analysis of why this bound is preferable or when it might fail.

Some baseline retraining (LlamaGen, VAR variants, DiT, DINOv2, ERM/RWY) is done by the authors due to lack of public checkpoints at matching settings, which, despite good-faith effort, introduces potential confounds when comparing across very different architectures/training pipelines.

Efficiency gains, while real, are somewhat expected: comparing NFEs of an AR model (which is inherently parallelizable/cheap per pass) against a diffusion model requiring many function evaluations is a known trade-off in the literature; the paper does not explore whether even fewer orders (K<20) with smarter/importance sampling could further close the efficiency-accuracy gap.

Comparisons to DINOv2 show mixed results (RandAR trails on ID accuracy and IN-A), so the "competitive with SOTA SSL" claim, while defensible, is not a clear win and depends on which benchmark is emphasized.

ImageNet-Val/Sketch/C evaluations are conducted on 2K-image subsets due to compute cost, and no variance/error bars are reported across runs or subsets, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of relatively small accuracy differences (e.g., <1% gaps in some rows of Table 2 and Table 6).

The novelty is essentially confined to a single underlying model family (RandAR); it is unclear how well the order-marginalization idea generalizes to other any-order or parallel-decoding AR architectures, limiting the generality of the claimed insight.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated central insight: fixed token order imposes a restrictive inductive bias on AR-based generative classifiers, and marginalizing over multiple orders using any-order AR models (RandAR) substantially improves classification accuracy and robustness.

Extensive and carefully controlled experiments: comparisons across model sizes (L/XL), multiple OOD benchmarks (IN-R/S/A/C), WILDS distribution-shift datasets, and efficiency-accuracy tradeoff curves against diffusion classifiers, giving a comprehensive picture of the method's advantages.

Novel and valuable comparison against strong self-supervised discriminative baselines (DINOv2), which prior generative-classifier literature has largely avoided, providing a more meaningful benchmark for judging the practical relevance of generative classifiers.

Thorough ablations (likelihood estimation strategy via Jensen's bound vs. direct estimate, tokenizer choice and noise augmentation, loss-weighting schemes for diffusion baselines, per-token/per-prefix-length analyses) that strengthen the empirical case and aid reproducibility.
Interesting qualitative analyses (per-token discriminative log-likelihood maps, error analysis comparing failure modes with DINOv2) that provide interpretability insight beyond raw accuracy numbers.
Efficiency gains (up to 25x faster than diffusion classifiers) combined with superior accuracy make the contribution practically relevant, not just an incremental accuracy bump.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is relatively lightweight: applying Monte Carlo order marginalization (with a Jensen's-inequality lower bound) to an existing any-order AR model (RandAR) for classification. This is a smart but incremental adaptation rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

All experiments rely on a single any-order AR backbone (RandAR); it is unclear how well the observed benefits (and the specific advantage of the lower-bound objective over the direct marginal likelihood) generalize to other any-order or parallel-decoding AR architectures.

The explanation for why the Jensen's-inequality lower bound significantly outperforms the direct order-marginal likelihood estimate is only a plausible hypothesis (alignment with the training objective) without deeper theoretical or ablation-based justification.

Discussion/comparison with the concurrent closely related A-VARC (VAR-based generative classifier with contrastive alignment) is fairly brief, given its similar motivation; a more detailed analysis of where and why the proposed approach differs and outperforms would strengthen the positioning.

The improvement from K=1 to larger K comes at proportional extra inference cost (K forward passes), and while still cheaper than diffusion classifiers, the paper could better characterize the accuracy/cost trade-off boundary for practitioners with tighter compute budgets.

Minor inconsistency in tokenizer choice across experiments (LlamaGen+noise-aug for main ImageNet results vs. MaskGIT for WILDS) is explained but slightly complicates direct comparison across sections.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated central insight: fixed token order imposes a restrictive inductive bias for AR-based generative classification, and order marginalization via any-order AR models (RandAR) substantially improves accuracy — this is demonstrated convincingly through Table 1 and the qualitative per-token analyses in Figs 3-5.

Strong and extensive empirical evaluation: comparisons against diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT, SiT+REPA), joint energy models (DAT), other AR baselines (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC+), discriminative supervised (ViT) and SOTA SSL (DINOv2) models, across in-domain and multiple OOD benchmarks (IN-R/S/A/C), plus WILDS distribution-shift datasets (Camelyon17, CelebA, FMoW) and non-image-centric/multi-object datasets (ObjectNet, COCO).

Good efficiency analysis showing up to 25x speedup over diffusion classifiers at comparable or better accuracy, with accuracy-vs-runtime curves across model sizes (Fig 6), which is a practically important contribution given DCs' expensive multi-step likelihood estimation.

Thoughtful ablations: likelihood estimation strategy (lower bound vs direct estimate, Table 5), tokenizer choice and noise augmentation (Tables 3-4), generalization to another any-order architecture (RAR, Table 6 left), and connection to masked diffusion models with theoretical derivation (Appendix D) plus empirical comparison (Table 6 right).

The comparison against SOTA self-supervised discriminative models (DINOv2) is a novel and meaningful benchmark that prior generative-classifier papers have not attempted, adding significance to the contribution.

Extensive appendices addressing many reviewer-anticipated concerns: DM noise averaging (Appendix C), loss weighting ablations for DM baselines (Appendix E), ResNet comparison (Appendix F), REPA variants (Appendix F), few-step diffusion (MeanFlow) comparison (Appendix I), and per-token likelihood importance analysis (Appendix B) — these substantially strengthen the fairness and thoroughness of the empirical claims.
Reasonably good clarity, with a clear framework diagram (Fig 2) and interesting qualitative visualizations of per-token discriminative likelihoods that support the core hypothesis.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: the method largely applies an existing any-order AR model (RandAR) with Monte Carlo averaging over the model's own training objective (Eq 5) to classification, without introducing new algorithmic machinery specific to classification (e.g., no learned order selection, no fine-tuning for discrimination). The 'lower bound over direct likelihood' insight is useful but relatively simple in nature.

RandAR-XL still underperforms DINOv2 on in-domain ImageNet accuracy and on IN-A, and the paper's claims of 'competitive' performance rely on cherry-picking specific OOD sets where RandAR wins (3 of 5); a more balanced framing of where generative classifiers still lag is warranted.

The efficiency comparison against diffusion classifiers, while extensive, focuses mainly on standard multi-step DMs; although Appendix I compares to MeanFlow, that comparison shows few-step diffusion classifiers perform much worse, which raises the question whether the diffusion baseline is representative of the strongest possible diffusion-based classifier design (e.g., more efficient ELBO estimators) rather than an artifact of insufficiently optimized few-step likelihood estimation.

K (number of sampled orders) must be fairly large (K=20) to achieve strong performance, which multiplies inference cost roughly 20x relative to a single AR forward pass; although this remains cheaper than DMs, the paper could better contextualize the practical cost/complexity tradeoff for users who might want single-pass efficiency.

The method depends on a specific any-order AR architecture (RandAR) with explicit position-token conditioning; generalization is only lightly validated with one additional architecture (RAR-B) at a single (base) model scale, leaving open questions about whether the approach scales across other any-order or masked generative architectures.

Some of the explanatory hypotheses (e.g., why per-token accuracy peaks at prefix length ~70, why raster order underperforms random K=1) are speculative post-hoc arguments without deeper causal or theoretical validation.

The experiments and analyses are entirely restricted to ImageNet-derived tasks (plus WILDS and COCO/ObjectNet variants at 256x256); scalability to higher-resolution or more complex/multi-domain benchmarks is unexplored, which somewhat limits the demonstrated generality of the classification improvements claimed.

strengths: Identifies and clearly demonstrates an important limitation of prior AR-based generative classifiers (fixed token order) with intuitive and convincing qualitative evidence (Fig. 1, 3, 4, 5).

The order-marginalization approach, grounded in a Jensen's-inequality lower bound rather than the naive marginal likelihood, is empirically well-motivated (Table 5) and the paper also provides a nice theoretical connection between any-order AR and masked diffusion ELBOs (Appendix D), unifying two generative classifier families.

Extensive and carefully controlled experimental comparison: multiple model scales (L/XL), multiple AR backbones (RandAR, RAR, LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC+), diffusion baselines (DiT, SiT, SiT+REPA, MeanFlow), SSL discriminative baselines (DINOv2), joint EBM baselines (DAT), and ResNet baselines, all trained under comparable settings for fairness.

Strong empirical results: order-marginalized RandAR consistently outperforms diffusion classifiers on ID and multiple OOD benchmarks while being up to 25x faster, and it is competitive with DINOv2 on several OOD sets — a genuinely interesting and previously unreported finding for generative classifiers.

Thorough ablation studies (tokenizer choice and noise augmentation, likelihood estimation strategy, per-token/prefix-length analyses, AR-vs-MD scoring, non-image-centric/multi-object datasets, real-world distribution shift on WILDS, loss-weighting ablations for diffusion baselines) that substantially strengthen the empirical case and reproducibility.
Honest error analysis (Fig. 7) and candid discussion of limitations (e.g., FID not correlating with classification accuracy, few-step diffusion models like MeanFlow underperforming as classifiers).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: the method largely consists of applying Monte Carlo order-marginalization to an existing any-order AR model (RandAR) for an existing task (generative classification), rather than introducing new architectures or training objectives; most of the paper's value lies in analysis and thorough benchmarking rather than algorithmic novelty.

The explanation for why the Jensen lower-bound estimate outperforms the direct marginal likelihood estimate is only hypothesized ("we hypothesize that... RandAR was trained directly on Eq. 5") rather than rigorously justified or tested with alternative training objectives.

The approach is demonstrated almost exclusively with RandAR as the primary backbone; although Section 6.6 shows generalization to RAR, this is only tested at the B-scale, limiting confidence that the method generalizes robustly across the broader space of any-order AR architectures and scales.
RandAR still trails DINOv2 on ImageNet-Val and notably on ImageNet-A, so the "competitive with SOTA SSL" claim is only partially supported and is sensitive to which OOD benchmark is emphasized.

Diffusion baselines (DiT/SiT) are not necessarily the strongest possible generative classifiers; while the authors do explore weighting schemes and REPA variants, the diffusion comparison could be seen as not fully exhaustive relative to the rapidly evolving space of diffusion/flow models, slightly weakening the "diffusion vs AR" framing of the paper's central claim.

Evaluation is restricted to relatively small-scale/moderate-resolution (256×256) ImageNet-family and WILDS benchmarks; it remains unclear how the approach scales to larger class counts, higher resolutions, or more complex real-world classification settings beyond the datasets tested.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear, well-motivated limitation of prior AR-based generative classifiers (fixed token order) and provides a simple, principled solution via order-marginalization using any-order AR models like RandAR, with a clean theoretical justification (Jensen's lower bound, and its equivalence to masked diffusion ELBO in Appendix D).

Strong and comprehensive experimental validation: results span in-domain ImageNet accuracy, multiple OOD benchmarks (IN-R/S/A/C), efficiency comparisons against diffusion classifiers (up to 25x speedup), comparisons against strong discriminative SSL baselines (DINOv2), joint energy models (DAT), and prior AR-based classifiers (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC+), as well as real-world distribution shift datasets (WILDS: Camelyon17, CelebA, FMoW).

Thorough ablation studies, including likelihood estimation strategy (lower bound vs direct estimate), tokenizer choice and robustness to noise augmentation, generalization to a second any-order architecture (RAR) to show the approach is not RandAR-specific, and AR vs masked-diffusion evaluation regimes.

Insightful analysis section (Section 5) with per-token accuracy/likelihood visualizations that build intuition for why order-marginalization helps (broader contextual coverage of discriminative image regions), and an honest error analysis comparing failure modes with DINOv2.

Extensive appendix strengthens the empirical case: comparisons to few-step diffusion (MeanFlow), REPA variants, ResNet baselines, non-image-centric/multi-object datasets (ObjectNet, COCO), and analysis decoupling generation quality (FID) from classification accuracy — this breadth substantially increases confidence in the robustness of the claims.
The efficiency argument is compelling and practically important, addressing a well-known bottleneck of diffusion-based generative classifiers.
Fair-comparison discipline is evident: authors control for model size, resolution, token count, and ablate loss-weighting choices for diffusion baselines to avoid strawman comparisons.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is somewhat incremental — it largely amounts to applying an existing any-order AR architecture (RandAR) to the classification setting with a straightforward Monte Carlo/Jensen lower-bound aggregation, rather than proposing fundamentally new modeling or training techniques.

Reliance on a single primary any-order backbone (RandAR) for most experiments; while RAR is used to show generalization (Section 6.6), this is only at the B-scale, leaving open how broadly the findings transfer across other any-order or order-conditioned AR architectures at larger scale.

The gap to DINOv2 in-domain accuracy (and clear loss on IN-A) is not fully explained beyond the general error analysis, and the paper does not explore whether increasing K beyond 20 or scaling model size further could close this gap, leaving the ceiling of the method somewhat unclear.

Computational cost, while much better than diffusion classifiers, is still non-trivial compared to discriminative baselines (K forward passes per class), and there is limited discussion of memory/throughput implications for the 1000-class ImageNet setting beyond single-image timing plots.

The theoretical explanation for why the Jensen lower bound outperforms the direct marginal likelihood estimate remains largely hypothesized ('we hypothesize that…') rather than rigorously established, leaving an open question about the underlying mechanism.

Some quantitative comparisons (e.g., A-VARC+, VAR reproductions) rely on the authors' own reimplementation/reproduction of baselines' pretraining pipelines, which, despite stated fidelity to official implementations, could introduce reproducibility discrepancies not fully controllable by third parties.
